newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - South Africans bank with beer and a chat.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - South Africans bank with beer and a chat.

text.p: A group of people drinking beer in the shade of a thorn tree might not appear a likely place for high finance.

But millions of black South Africans do their banking in these surroundings, ploughing their wages into "stokvels" -- informal savings clubs that meet for a brew and a chat or perhaps a prayer, while they dream of what to do with the cash.
Most stokvels, an expression deriving from rotating cattle auctions or stock fairs in the last century, meet weekly or monthly with members contributing set amounts each time.
Tithes, commonly from 50 to 80 rand ($10.7 to $17.2), are pooled and then given to each "stockfeller" in turn.
It is a way to save for something worthwhile that would remain a dream if the small sums were frittered away.

Stoves, video machines, furniture or even cars count among goods members might want to buy for cash, avoiding the high costs of hire purchase agreements in South Africa, where the prime lending rate is 19.25 percent.
Mohau Phatlane, of the National Stokvels Association of South Africa, said black people are increasingly using banks, but still rely on goodwill in times of need.
Many groups operate as burial societies where members save to ensure a decent send-off from a culture prizing lavish funerals which can leave relatives destitute.

"It is based on ubuntu (human-heartedness and goodness). People trust and believe in each other. It could be through school or church or work, but you always deal with people you know," Phatlane said in an interview.

He said his association formed part of the link between informal and formal banking in South Africa, advising members on investments such as unit trusts or mutual funds, as well as negotiating preferential rates on death benefit schemes with life assurers.
"We would like to see people not keeping their money under their beds. It is important to teach people to bank," he said.
Stokvels usually range in size from four to 20 members but some, like the Great North Burial Society, count thousands of contributors.
Phatlane's association claims to group several million members in hundreds of thousands of stokvels.
Aaron Tengani, of market research company Markinor, said this was almost impossible to verify, but that stokvel savings were estimated at over 700 million rand each year.
"In the past it has been extremely difficult to assess. Many groups are a loose sort of arrangement," he told Reuters.
Many stokvel members save for Christmas, the main spending season, when migrant labourers travel from the cities back to their families in villages often hundreds of kilometres (miles) away.
They have to pay for transport and are expected to bring gifts for relatives hoping for summer holiday treats.
Other have more hedonistic motives, saving up for wild parties or "gumbas" where they slaughter sheep and buy liquor for their friends.
The celebrations, called after the pulsating music that is essential to attracting free-spenders, can last a whole weekend, with the hosts selling beer and food to increase their returns.

The country's biggest daily newspaper, Sowetan, has a column on Fridays to announce stokvel parties on the go at the homes of members of savings clubs with names like The Shepherd, the Peace Club, China Gardens or Savuka (Get up).
"When it is a stokvel party we wear pants," says Margaret Moloto, who is not a club member, but supports her friends when they throw gumbas in Soweto.
"We can't wear dresses, because we dance too wildly."
One of the problems facing stokvels is pyramid schemes which depend on an endless source of new members to pay big sums to those who joined earlier.
When these run out of new recruits they collapse, bringing misery and suspicion that can taint all stokvels, Phatlane said.

The central Reserve Bank, which oversees the most sophisticated financial infrastructure on the continent, also keeps an eye on stokvels, setting a 9.9 million rand limit on the deposits they can hold.
But Phatlane said negotiations were under way for changes.
"As far as we are concerned, as long as (a stokvel) is legitimate, it does not matter how much money they are investing." ($1=4.65 rand)
